blocks.text: A 58-year-old man with pneumonia is on 15 L/min of oxygen through a reservoir mask, breathing at 34 per minute and tiring, with a saturation of 88 per cent. The question for the intensive care team is not only what is wrong, but which kind of organ support he needs, and how much harm each kind can cause.

blocks.markdown: Critical care supports failing organs while the underlying disease is treated. Respiratory support ranges from oxygen therapy through **non-invasive ventilation (NIV)** to **invasive mechanical ventilation** via a tracheal tube. Circulatory support uses fluids, **vasopressors** and **inotropes**, guided by **invasive monitoring**. Every form of support has risks, so the aim is the least invasive support that is effective, and a clear plan to wean it.

blocks.title: NIV and invasive ventilation
blocks.text: NIV delivers positive pressure through a tight-fitting mask or hood: CPAP gives a single continuous pressure; bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) gives a higher inspiratory and a lower expiratory pressure and so assists ventilation. Invasive ventilation delivers breaths through an endotracheal tube, with the patient sedated and paralysed if needed.

rows: Patient's own airway, must protect it
Hypercapnic COPD exacerbation (BiPAP), acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (CPAP)
Failed NIV, GCS too low to protect the airway, exhaustion, severe hypoxaemia, shock needing support
Mask intolerance, aspiration, delay to intubation
Ventilator-associated pneumonia, lung injury, sedation, tube complications
Clinical review and blood gas after 1 to 2 hours
blocks.caption: Comparing respiratory support (see British Thoracic Society and ICS guidance for current criteria)

blocks.markdown: In a COPD exacerbation with respiratory acidosis (for example a pH below about 7.35 with raised PaCO2) persisting after initial medical treatment, BiPAP reduces the need for intubation. It requires a patient who can protect the airway and cooperate, and a clear escalation plan agreed in advance, including whether intubation is appropriate. NIV failure is suggested by worsening gas exchange, exhaustion, falling consciousness or intolerance, and delaying intubation in such patients is harmful. Check current BTS/NICE criteria and local protocols.

items: Indications for intubation and invasive ventilation: inability to protect or maintain the airway, failure of NIV or of oxygen therapy, severe respiratory failure or exhaustion, shock or cardiac arrest, and need for airway control for procedures.
Early and senior airway help is crucial because induction of anaesthesia in a critically ill patient can cause profound hypotension and hypoxaemia.
After intubation, ventilate with lung-protective settings and monitor gases, pressures and haemodynamics.

blocks.markdown: **Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)** is acute inflammatory lung injury with increased permeability pulmonary oedema, causing severe hypoxaemia and stiff lungs. The **Berlin definition** requires: onset within 1 week of a known insult or new or worsening respiratory symptoms; bilateral opacities on chest imaging not fully explained by effusions, collapse or nodules; respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload; and impaired oxygenation measured by the **PaO2/FiO2 ratio** (P/F ratio) on a minimum PEEP of 5 cmH2O. Severity bands in mmHg are mild (above 200 to 300), moderate (above 100 to 200) and severe (100 or less). Common causes include pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration and pancreatitis.

blocks.caption: PaO2: arterial oxygen tension in mmHg; FiO2: fraction of inspired oxygen as a decimal (0.21 to 1.0)

blocks.title: Grading oxygenation impairment
blocks.prompt: A ventilated patient with bilateral opacities after aspiration has PaO2 85 mmHg on FiO2 0.40 with PEEP 8 cmH2O. Calculate the P/F ratio and band.

steps.text: A value above 200 and up to 300, on PEEP of at least 5, falls in the mild Berlin band.
Check the other criteria: onset within a week of the insult, bilateral opacities, and not explained by cardiac failure; then classify as mild ARDS, and treat the cause.
Reassess regularly, because the P/F ratio can worsen quickly and the band changes management.

blocks.answer: P/F about 212, mild ARDS band (if other Berlin criteria are met); reassess regularly.

blocks.markdown: **Lung-protective ventilation** limits ventilator-induced lung injury. The ARDSNet approach used a tidal volume of about 6 mL per kg of **predicted body weight (PBW)**, which depends on height and sex rather than actual weight, and limits plateau pressure (a commonly quoted limit is 30 cmH2O; check current guidance). In severe ARDS, prone positioning for prolonged periods and neuromuscular blockade in selected patients improve survival, as taught in current guidelines.

blocks.title: Tidal volume per predicted body weight
blocks.prompt: A woman of height 165 cm has ARDS. Calculate her PBW and a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg (check current ventilation guidance).

steps.text: Use PBW rather than actual weight because lung size depends on height and sex; actual weight would over-distend the lungs in an obese patient.

blocks.answer: PBW about 57 kg; tidal volume about 342 mL (6 mL/kg PBW).

blocks.markdown: **Circulatory support.** In shock that persists despite fluids, **vasopressors** raise blood pressure by increasing vascular tone. **Norepinephrine (noradrenaline)** acts mainly on alpha-1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction, with some beta-1 effect, and is the usual first-line vasopressor in septic shock; vasopressin may be added. **Inotropes** such as dobutamine increase contractility when cardiac output is low. Vasopressors are titrated to a target such as a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg (individualised), infused through a central venous catheter where possible, and extravasation of a peripheral infusion can cause tissue necrosis. Concentrations, doses and targets vary; check local protocols.

blocks.title: Invasive monitoring
blocks.text: An arterial line gives beat-to-beat blood pressure and allows repeated blood gas sampling, which is essential while titrating vasopressors. A central venous catheter allows reliable vasopressor delivery, central venous pressure and central venous oxygen saturation measurement, but carries risks of infection, pneumothorax and thrombosis. Monitoring supports decisions; it does not replace clinical assessment.

points: NIV suits conscious cooperative patients with hypercapnic COPD (BiPAP) or cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (CPAP); failure should prompt timely intubation.
Invasive ventilation is indicated for airway failure, NIV failure, exhaustion, severe hypoxaemia or shock, and requires lung-protective settings.
ARDS is defined by Berlin criteria with P/F bands; use about 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, not actual weight.
Vasopressors, chiefly norepinephrine, restore vascular tone, guided by arterial and central venous monitoring (check local protocols).

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with COPD has a pH of 7.27 and a PaCO2 of 9.2 kPa one hour after maximal medical therapy. He is alert and cooperative. What is the most appropriate next step, according to usual BTS-style teaching?

options.text: Start BiPAP non-invasive ventilation with an agreed escalation plan
Increase oxygen to 15 L/min and observe
Immediate intubation without a trial of NIV
Give oral antibiotics and discharge

questions.correctOptionText: Start BiPAP non-invasive ventilation with an agreed escalation plan

distractorRationale.a: Correct: persistent hypercapnic acidosis in an alert patient is the classic indication for BiPAP.
distractorRationale.b: High-flow oxygen can worsen hypercapnia and does not address ventilation.
distractorRationale.c: Intubation is not first-line when NIV is suitable.
distractorRationale.d: This patient needs acute respiratory support.

questions.explanation: BiPAP assists ventilation, lowers PaCO2 and reduces the need for intubation in hypercapnic exacerbations. A decision on ceiling of care and escalation should be made before starting, and the response is checked on repeat gases; check current guidance.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old with severe pneumonia on BiPAP becomes exhausted, drowsy and has a rising PaCO2 and falling pH after 2 hours. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Urgent senior assessment for intubation and invasive ventilation
Continue the same settings for another 12 hours
Switch to a lower oxygen concentration
Remove the mask and give an oral sedative

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent senior assessment for intubation and invasive ventilation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: worsening gas exchange, drowsiness and exhaustion indicate NIV failure.
distractorRationale.b: Persisting with failing NIV risks arrest.
distractorRationale.c: Reducing oxygen does not address ventilatory failure.

questions.explanation: Reduced consciousness and rising PaCO2 mean the patient cannot protect the airway or sustain breathing. Delay increases the risk of emergency intubation under worse conditions, so escalate early with senior airway help.

questions.stem: What is the principal action of norepinephrine (noradrenaline) used to treat septic shock?

options.text: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction that raises systemic vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure
Pure beta-2 mediated bronchodilation
Blockade of calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle
Reduction of circulating volume by diuresis

questions.correctOptionText: Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction that raises systemic vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: norepinephrine mainly stimulates alpha-1 receptors with some beta-1 effect.
distractorRationale.b: Beta-2 bronchodilation is characteristic of salbutamol, not norepinephrine.
distractorRationale.c: Calcium channel blockers lower blood pressure.

questions.explanation: Septic shock features vasodilatation, so restoring vascular tone is the aim. Norepinephrine acts on alpha-1 receptors to constrict vessels, with some beta-1 inotropic effect, and is titrated to a MAP target.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock requires a norepinephrine infusion titrated against frequent blood gases. Which monitoring is most appropriate?

options.text: An arterial line for continuous blood pressure and sampling, and central venous access for the infusion
Four-hourly manual blood pressure with a cuff
No monitoring beyond pulse oximetry
Daily weight only

questions.correctOptionText: An arterial line for continuous blood pressure and sampling, and central venous access for the infusion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: vasopressor titration requires beat-to-beat blood pressure and reliable venous access.
distractorRationale.b: Intermittent cuff readings are too infrequent while titrating vasopressors.
distractorRationale.c: Pulse oximetry alone cannot guide blood pressure management.
distractorRationale.d: Weight is not an adequate monitor in acute shock.

questions.explanation: Vasopressor doses are adjusted quickly, so continuous arterial pressure is needed. A central line allows safer delivery of vasoactive drugs, though risks such as infection and pneumothorax are accepted and local protocols may allow a peripheral start.

questions.stem: Which patient best fulfils the Berlin definition of ARDS?

options.text: Onset 3 days after aspiration, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 of 150 mmHg on PEEP 8 cmH2O, and no evidence of heart failure
Unilateral lobar consolidation with PaO2/FiO2 of 350 mmHg
Bilateral opacities with a raised JVP, oedema and a low ejection fraction, fully explained by heart failure
Symptoms present for 6 weeks with normal oxygenation

questions.correctOptionText: Onset 3 days after aspiration, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 of 150 mmHg on PEEP 8 cmH2O, and no evidence of heart failure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acute onset, bilateral opacities, impaired oxygenation on PEEP and no cardiac explanation.
distractorRationale.b: Unilateral disease with a P/F above 300 does not meet the criteria.
distractorRationale.c: Failure fully explained by cardiac failure excludes ARDS.
distractorRationale.d: A 6-week course and normal oxygenation do not meet the criteria.

questions.explanation: The Berlin definition requires onset within a week of an insult, bilateral opacities, respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure, and a P/F ratio of 300 mmHg or less on PEEP of at least 5. The patient described meets all of these, with a P/F in the moderate band.

questions.stem: Which statement about lung-protective ventilation in ARDS is correct?

options.text: Tidal volumes are based on predicted body weight, about 6 mL/kg, rather than actual weight
Tidal volumes should be 12 to 15 mL/kg of actual weight to improve gas exchange
Plateau pressure should be maximised
PEEP is avoided in ARDS

questions.correctOptionText: Tidal volumes are based on predicted body weight, about 6 mL/kg, rather than actual weight

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lung size depends on height and sex, so PBW is used.
distractorRationale.b: Large tidal volumes cause ventilator-induced lung injury.
distractorRationale.c: High plateau pressures contribute to injury and are limited.
distractorRationale.d: PEEP is a core component of ARDS ventilation.

questions.explanation: ARDS lungs have a small volume of aerated lung ('baby lung'), so large breaths over-distend it. Tidal volume is set per kg of predicted body weight, typically starting near 6 mL/kg with a limit on plateau pressure, as guided by current protocols.

questions.stem: A patient with bilateral opacities after sepsis has PaO2 70 mmHg on FiO2 0.60 with PEEP 10 cmH2O. Calculate the PaO2/FiO2 ratio. Give your answer in mmHg to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: P/F = 70 / 0.60 = 116.7, or about 117 mmHg. This lies between 100 and 200, which is the moderate band of the Berlin definition when the other criteria are met.

questions.stem: A man of height 180 cm is ventilated for ARDS. Using PBW (male) = 50 + 0.91 x (height in cm - 152.4) kg, calculate the tidal volume at 6 mL/kg of PBW. Give your answer in mL.
questions.explanation: Height above 152.4 cm is 27.6 cm, so PBW = 50 + 0.91 x 27.6 = 75.1 kg. Tidal volume = 6 x 75.1 = about 451 mL. PBW is used instead of actual weight because lung size is determined by height and sex.

questions.stem: Compare non-invasive and invasive ventilation, giving indications, requirements and risks of each, and explain how you decide when NIV has failed.
markingGuide: NIV: BiPAP for hypercapnic COPD exacerbation with acidosis after medical therapy; CPAP for cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
NIV requires a conscious, cooperative patient who can protect the airway and a pre-agreed escalation plan.
NIV risks: mask intolerance, aspiration, gastric distension and delay to intubation.
Invasive ventilation indications: failure of NIV or oxygen, inability to protect airway, exhaustion, severe hypoxaemia, shock or arrest.
Invasive risks: haemodynamic compromise at induction, ventilator-associated pneumonia, lung injury, sedation complications.
NIV failure: worsening gases, exhaustion, reduced consciousness, intolerance, no improvement within 1 to 2 hours of treatment.
questions.explanation: NIV avoids the risks of intubation but only works in the right patient. Early recognition of failure prevents a crash intubation.

questions.stem: Explain the basic principles of vasopressor use in shock and the role of arterial and central venous catheters in monitoring and delivery.
markingGuide: Vasopressors restore vascular tone and mean arterial pressure after adequate fluid resuscitation.
Norepinephrine is first-line in septic shock, acting mainly on alpha-1 receptors; vasopressin may be added; inotropes such as dobutamine increase contractility.
Titrated to a MAP target, commonly at least 65 mmHg, individualised.
Arterial line provides continuous blood pressure and sampling for gases.
Central venous catheter allows reliable vasopressor delivery, CVP and central venous oxygen saturation; risks include infection, pneumothorax, thrombosis.
Extravasation of peripheral infusions can cause necrosis; follow local protocols.
questions.explanation: Vasopressors only work after restoring volume and need careful titration. Invasive monitoring helps safe titration but carries risks.
